records.summary: Breaches in hulls and open spaces expose characters to vacuum. Without a space suit, they must hold their breath (Constitution modifier + 1 rounds) before suffocating. Decompression damage is 1d8 per round if exposed suddenly to open space.

Certain pathways are blocked by collapsed debris or broken machinery, forcing players to find alternate routes or clear the obstruction with Strength checks (DC 14). Clearing paths can make noise, alerting potential threats. Resting on an Abandoned Space Station

Small gravitational fields from celestial bodies or intense magnetic pulls may shift characters off course. Overcoming these forces requires Strength checks (DC 14) or thrusters to stabilize movement.

Pirates and scavengers use the nebula as cover to ambush passing ships or explore hidden resources. Characters must make Dexterity saving throws (DC 15) to avoid surprise attacks, or Charisma (Intimidation) checks (DC 14) to negotiate safe passage.

Sudden drops in pressure create dangerous downward currents, pulling objects or individuals deeper into the atmosphere. Escaping requires Dexterity (Acrobatics) or Strength (Athletics) checks (DC 15) to break free or stabilize.

Sections of the city suffer from decaying infrastructure. Roll a d20 each hour; on a 1-3, characters encounter broken lifts, malfunctioning doors, or unstable walkways, requiring Dexterity saving throws (DC 12) to avoid injury.

Characters need to monitor air filters and pressure levels, particularly if their equipment isnʼt designed for high-pressure or toxic gas environments. Every 4 hours, roll a d20; on a 5 or lower, equipment requires repairs or filters must be replaced.

1.Asteroid Collisions: Roll a d20 every 10 minutes. On a 1-4, an asteroid moves dangerously close to the player or ship, requiring Dexterity saving throws (DC 15) to dodge. Failure results in 2d6 bludgeoning damage, with larger asteroids causing 4d6 damage. 2.Radiation Pockets: Certain regions in the field emit high levels of radiation. Entering a radiation zone requires Constitution saving throws (DC 14) every 10 minutes to avoid radiation poisoning and 1 level of exhaustion.

1.Crushing Gravitational Pull: Entering certain zones too close to the black hole subjects characters to intense gravity, risking severe compression damage. Every round within a critical zone, characters must make Constitution saving throws (DC 16) or suffer 3d6 bludgeoning damage as gravitational forces press down on them.

The stationʼs crowded environment can be exhausting. Characters who spend more than 8 hours in high-traffic areas without rest must make a Constitution saving throw (DC 12) to avoid fatigue (1 level of exhaustion).

1.Station Layout: •Darkened Halls and Corridors: Many sections lack lighting, requiring players to rely on flashlights or other light sources. •Maintenance Tunnels: Small, cramped spaces offering shortcuts but prone to malfunctions, sudden air leaks, or nests of scavenger creatures. •Control Rooms and Terminals: Vital access points for station information, but often damaged, requiring repairs to function. •Containment Labs or Medical Bays: Facilities for scientific or medical research that may contain useful equipment or hazards, like broken containment fields or biological samples. •Cargoholds and Storage Bays: Large areas with scattered supplies but prone to air leaks, unstable stacks of crates, and broken machinery. 2.Environmental Conditions: •Limited Lighting: The stationʼs lighting systems are mostly offline, reducing visibility to 10 feet in dark areas. Areas with occasional flickering lights impose disadvantage on Perception checks relying on sight. •Artificial Gravity Fluctuations: The stationʼs gravity is unstable, occasionally switching off. When it does, characters must succeed on Dexterity saving throws (DC 12) or drift in zero gravity. •Stale or Thin Air: The air circulation system is partially offline, requiring Constitution saving throws (DC 13) every hour to avoid fatigue or low-level oxygen deprivation.

1.Travel Pace: •Slow: ½ mile per hour, allowing for precise navigation and data collection •Normal: 1 mile per hour •Fast: 2 miles per hour (increased risk of being pulled into a gravitational shear zone or encountering time dilation effects) 2.Navigating Gravitational Shears: •Ships navigating near gravitational shear zones must make Dexterity (Piloting) checks (DC 15) every 10 minutes. Failure results in loss of control, pulling the ship closer to the black hole or subjecting it to intense gravitational forces. •Individuals moving in this area must succeed on Dexterity (Acrobatics) checks (DC 14) or be pulled off course, drifting dangerously closer to the black holeʼs pull.
Each hour, characters must make Constitution saving throws (DC 13) to avoid the long-term effects of radiation and time dilation, which may result in hallucinations or weakened cognitive abilities.

Access to clean water, filtered air, and other essentials is often limited in lower levels. Characters spending more than 8 hours in low-resource areas must make Constitution saving throws (DC 12) to avoid 1 level of exhaustion.

Short rests can be taken in public seating areas, private quarters (if available), or other safe spaces. Characters in public areas must make Wisdom (Perception) checks (DC 12) to avoid pickpockets or interruptions.

1.Radiation Exposure: Space is filled with cosmic radiation. Each hour in open space, characters without radiation protection must make a Constitution saving throw (DC 14) or suffer 1 level of exhaustion from radiation sickness. 2.Micrometeor Impacts: Tiny, high-velocity particles travel through space, posing a constant risk. Roll a d20 every hour in the void; on a 1, characters must make Dexterity saving throws (DC 15) to avoid 1d10 piercing damage from micrometeor impacts.

•Mild (0–4 hours): No immediate effect. •Moderate (4–24 hours): Roll for minor side effects; mild hallucinations or disorientation. •Severe (24+ hours): Must begin making Mutation Checks (see table), or spend XP on Adaptation Perks. GMs should track exposure passively and inform players when thresholds are reached. Sudden or extreme exposure (e.g., a foldstorm, reality rupture) may count as automatic severe exposure. 🌟 Chaos Adaptation Perk Tree (Tiers 1–5) Players can spend XP to evolve under the influence of the Foam and Chaos. These perks reflect biological, mental, or metaphysical changes that allow survival, travel, and power acquisition in these realms. Prerequisites are listed below each tier. All perks are optional unless required to resist a mutation. Tier 1 – Initiate Adaptations

In both the Foam and Chaos, resources exist—but theyʼre unpredictable. •No Natural Decay: Organic material doesn't rot, which means food lasts—but also doesnʼt replenish. •Water and Air: May be breathable but often stagnant, toxic, or illusionary. •Foraging: Characters can attempt foraging using Survival, Arcana, or relevant Knowledge skills, with DCs based on zone stability. ◦ Chaos-forged fruit, crystal fungi, or inverted meat-plants may be edible—or transformative. •Scavenging: Ruins in both realms often yield relics, components, or anomalous objects. Caution: Eating unprocessed materials may invoke random magical or biological effects. The GM may call for a Chaos Effect roll on a scavenged item table.
Used to resist chaos distortions and determine how well your character adapts to shifting reality. Stability Check = Wisdom or Constitution save, DC 12–18 depending on intensity.

Time inside the Chaos and Foam does not match time outside. You may experience days while the outside world moves in minutes—or vice versa. •Standard Rule: 1 hour in the Chaos = 6 hours in the Sea of Realities (or GM-defined distortion). •Flicker Zones and Stasis Fields may pause or scramble time entirely. •Time-sensitive missions must account for this, and parties may return to find centuries have passed.
"You wonʼt hear it coming. If you see one, thereʼs already more."

The Gray Sands is an existential horror setting where silence is oppressive, reality is fragile, and the self is at risk of being forgotten. Whether players are searching for lost knowledge, escaping something far worse, or simply trying to find color in a colorless world, the Gray Sands will change them—if they survive. Would you like an encounter table or special mechanics for navigation and survival? Here are the stat blocks for the inhabitants of the Gray Sands, designed for Multiversal using a balanced mix of horror, psychological warfare, and environmental threats.
"They float like dust in the wind, but when they touch you, you forget why you ever left home."

•Bound to Their Path: They cannot move beyond the area where they were first encountered. •True Names Banish Them: If a player speaks their original name aloud (even in writing), they instantly turn to dust.

Mechanic: Cause and effect no longer function predictably, resulting in random outcomes. Whenever players attempt an action, roll a d4: 1: The outcome is completely different from what they intended. 2: The outcome is successful, but with a strange twist. 3: The outcome fails but offers a surprising, unrelated benefit. 4: The action succeeds as intended. Interpretation: GMs can use these results to add unpredictable elements, such as doors leading to unexpected places or objects behaving in unusual ways.

Mechanic: Solid structures become fluid and shapeless, making it hard to tell what is stable. Stability Checks: Players must make Wisdom (Perception) checks (DC 13) to identify stable areas before moving. Failure results in stepping onto unstable terrain, requiring a Dexterity saving throw (DC 12) to avoid slipping or sinking into the dissolving ground. Shifting Perceptions: Players may experience blurred vision or mild hallucinations when viewing amorphous objects for prolonged periods, adding -1 to Perception checks.

- Encounter: Guardian entities bound to the slumbering gods protect their realms, enforcing the boundary between existence and Oblivion. These beings appear only when travelers approach the gods directly. - Interaction Check: Players must make Charisma (Persuasion or Intimidation) checks (DC 18) to gain favor or avoid hostility. - Consequences of Failure: Failing to convince the guardians may result in temporary disadvantage on all Wisdom-based checks as players feel overwhelmed by the guardians' presence.

•In rare cases, parts of a characterʼs consciousness and body may be split, causing simultaneous but uncoordinated actions. ◦ Resolution: The DM may require dual checks (a combined DC 15 Wisdom and Athletics check) to re-align the two aspects. Failure may result in narrative complications—such as being partially stranded in one realm—until resolved.

◦ To exit the Dreaming Realms and enter the outer layers of the multiverse, a character in physical mode must find a “Cosmic Gateway”—a transitional portal that is only accessible when traveling with their body.

Mechanic: Players can attempt to alter minor elements in the environment with a successful Charisma (Performance) check (DC 12). Effects: Changes last for 1d4 hours and can be anything from altering the color of the sky to creating a small object. Lucid Attention: Significant changes (e.g., creating large structures or drastically altering the environment) may attract the attention of lucid entities who patrol the realm. These entities may be friendly, curious, or hostile.

Mechanic: Shards drift constantly, impacting travel time between locations. Travel Time: Roll a d6 every hour of travel: 1-2: Travel time is halved. 3-4: Travel time is normal. 5-6: Travel time doubles, as shards drift out of alignment, forcing characters to detour or wait. Unstable Routes: GMs can use this mechanic to create encounters or force players to make difficult choices, such as jumping between distant shards or improvising routes.

Mechanic: Faint sounds or visual traces occasionally drift through Vacuousia, offering clues or faint memories of previous realms. Insight Checks: Players may make Wisdom (Insight) checks (DC 14) to gain brief insights or temporary bonuses (e.g., recalling a useful skill or gaining a +1 to a skill check for 10 minutes). Insubstantial Echoes: Echoes fade quickly, requiring players to act fast to capture their essence. Missing an echo may require waiting another hour for another to appear.

- Mechanic: Characters must secure a tether to anchor themselves against the pull of Oblivion. This tether could be an item with deep personal significance or a constructed anchor with an intent to survive. - Tether Check: Creating or locating a tether requires Wisdom (Survival) checks (DC 15) or Intelligence (Arcana) checks (DC 17). Tethers help characters resist the pull of Oblivion and reduce exhaustion checks to every two hours. - Current Toward Oblivion: Characters who lack a tether or lose their tether are pulled an additional 5 feet per hour toward Oblivion, increasing exhaustion risk and difficulty of navigation. ---

Mechanic: Entities within Deliquium resonate with strong emotions, reacting to charactersʼ feelings. Interaction: Players can attempt Charisma (Persuasion) checks (DC 13) to convert these resonant entities into allies or guides. Emotional Drain: Each interaction with an entity carries an emotional cost; characters must make Wisdom saving throws (DC 14) to avoid taking 1d4 psychic damage after each encounter as emotions drain.

In Visium, keep things relatively stable, but introduce small dream-like inconsistencies (e.g., a staircase that seems longer than it should or items that change colors when looked at from different angles). Visium should feel familiar yet slightly “off.”

Mechanic: The vast, featureless void of Vacuousia gradually drains the energy of those within it. Fatigue Check: Every 2 hours, players must make Constitution saving throws (DC 15) to avoid gaining a level of exhaustion. Fatigue Effects: GMs can vary the effects of this fatigue, applying disadvantage on Wisdom or Intelligence checks, or limiting movement speed, as the void wears down physical resilience and mental focus. Disorientation from Silence: Mechanic: The unnatural silence disrupts mental focus, making it difficult to remain alert. Silence Penalty: All Intelligence-based checks take a -2 penalty due to the disorienting silence and vastness, which dulls concentration. Temporary Sound Anchors: Players who succeed on Wisdom (Perception) checks (DC 15) may occasionally pick up faint sounds, briefly granting +1 to Perception checks and restoring their sense of orientation.

- Translimina may trap players in endless hallways. To find an exit, characters must succeed on a sequence of Intelligence (Investigation) and Wisdom (Insight) checks (DC 16) over the course of several hours, recognizing subtle patterns or changes. ---

- Ghostly Observers: Half-real entities linger around players, subtly affecting them. Players may feel watched or find themselves mimicked by shadowy figures. Failing a Charisma saving throw (DC 14) causes a temporary -1 penalty to Wisdom-based checks, representing a growing unease. - Reflected Self: At times, players may encounter faint, ghostly versions of themselves, mirroring their actions. Interacting with these “echoes” requires Charisma (Persuasion) or Wisdom (Insight) checks (DC 15) to avoid taking psychic damage (1d4) from the disorienting experience.

Mechanic: Ghostly, incomplete entities drift across the shards, remnants of individuals or creatures splintered by the realm. Interaction: Players may attempt to communicate with these entities using Charisma-based checks (DC 14). Successful interactions reveal fragments of information, navigation clues, or minor buffs (e.g., temporary Advantage on a skill check). Risk: Failed checks may cause these entities to become confused or hostile, imposing disadvantage on Charisma-based skills for 1 hour.

- Encounter: Characters may encounter faint, distorted versions of themselves, reflecting memories or emotions. Players can interact with these reflections through Wisdom (Insight) checks (DC 14) to gain insights into their subconscious thoughts or recall forgotten memories. - Risk: Repeated interaction may confuse players, who must make Intelligence saving throws (DC 14) to avoid temporarily believing they are the reflection rather than their real self. ---
